en: Title: *Vajrāmṛtatantra* Published: Sferra forthcoming 2017 Source:
CUL manuscript; some lemmata from Śrībhānu’s commentary.

[Chapter 1: Instruction on the Manifestation of the Secret Maṇḍala] Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling within the secret lotuses of the nectar-vajras of the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
The Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, sports together with Māmakī in the city.
There, that goddess, established in the secret [teaching], asks him.
(1.1) Śrībhānu: "In the secret" (*rahasye*) means being situated apart from other deities such as the Bodhisattvas. The particle *tu* has the sense of "indeed" (*satyarthe*).
"O Lord, you previously spoke of the supreme *Vajrāmṛta* Tantra;
O Great Bliss, tell us the means for accomplishing that nectar.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Great Bliss of Vajrāmṛta.
Inconceivable, imperishable, subtle, unfailing, and devoid of sense faculties—
supremely peaceful and utterly pure— it is proclaimed as Vajrāmṛta.
Then the Blessed One, the Holder of the Vajra, by means of the Vajrāmṛta samādhis, [attained it].

Māmakī, being filled with passion, has revealed the secret. (1.4) Śrībhānu asks: "What did she say? and replies: "By means of the *vajrāmṛta-samādhi*," and so forth. By means of the *vajrāmṛta-samādhi*, acting as either the agent or the cause, that secret reality (*tattva*) was revealed.
This supreme *vajrāmṛta*-knowledge, which has been concealed in all the tantras, [is now disclosed].
Therefore, I shall explain it through firm embraces and kisses,
through the union of amorous play, and through the transformations of song and instrumental music;
in this way, the supreme *Vajrāmṛta* Tantra is accomplished without delay.

Śrībhānu: It is served; it is accomplished by these causes; the meaning is that it shall become the object of manifestation. "Soon" means immediately after the kissing and so forth. "O Goddess" is used as a form of address. To the question "What is served?", he says: "The Tantra," and so on.
"O fair-faced one, for the sake of your pleasure, I shall speak of its accomplishment (*sādhana*);
I shall tell it in brief—listen to what I have spoken. (1.7)
For the benefit of all sentient beings, [I shall teach] the supreme nectar of yoga-practice;
by knowing which, a yogin is swiftly liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.
(1.8) Śrībhānu: "Yoga" refers to the yoga with the deity. Within that as well, "yoga" means meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); for that purpose, it is the "nectar," the essential core.
This great gnosis is not to be disclosed; it is the accomplishment that achieves the three worlds, bringing happiness to practitioners for the sake of attaining perfection of body, speech, and mind.
Śrībhānu: "Siddham" refers to the accomplishment of the subject at hand; [it is the accomplishment that achieves the three worlds].
"Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, one should kiss the bhaga-lotus that arises from the vajra-nectar; Māmakī, in turn, should kiss the vajra.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the great bliss of vajra-nectar.
Then, however, [fols.
2–5 missing] [Chapter 2: Instruction on the Knowledge of Reality and Yoga;
Chapter 3: Instruction on the Origination of Mantras]
The utterance of *svāhā*, however, bestows all accomplishments upon Māmakī. (3.20ab) [Chapter 4: Instruction on the Ritual of Homa] % Verses 13–18 restored from the *Sādhanamālā* 180.
Then the mantra-practitioner should mark out [the site] according to the dimensions of the fire-pit (homakuṇḍa).
For a rite of pacification (śāntika), it should be made circular; one should measure it to be one cubit in size.
One should dig half a cubit into the ground and have it colored white.
Having drawn a circular shape all around on both sides,
one should then dig a pit two cubits deep for nourishing rites (*pauṣṭika*), or one cubit deep.
It should be drawn as a square on all sides using yellow ochre.
For rites of sorcery (*abhicāruka*), one should dig a triangular pit twenty finger-breadths in width and draw [within it] a circle filled with garlands of flames measuring fifteen finger-breadths.
Likewise, for the purposes of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should likewise draw a half-moon.
The sacrificial fire-pit has been described; one should specify its orientation according to the directions.
Facing north, the mantra-practitioner should begin the rite for pacification (śāntika);
for prosperity (pauṣṭika), always in the east; and for malevolent rites (abhicāra) in the south.
In the south and the west, subjugation is said to be performed, as well as summoning and expulsion;
for malevolent rites it is always black, while for the two types of subjugation it is five-colored.
For rites of pacification (śāntika) and prosperity (pauṣṭika), one should offer oblations consisting of sesame, rice, milk, ghee, and honey, combined with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
and likewise all sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) from milky trees and fragrant trees.
One should offer various kinds of edible food, or the bali-offering for all spirits (sarvabhautika).
Whatever bali-offering is given by practitioners with the mudrās of Heruka,
whatever is desired by the mind is always accomplished for the yogin.
The practitioner should perform pacifying rites in the autumn, nourishing rites in the winter,
and all rites of sorcery in the summer.
Pacifying is said to be performed at dusk, and likewise, nourishing at dawn.
One should always perform the rite of sorcery (*abhicāruka*) at midday or at midnight.
Having generated one's own deity within the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*,
and having meditated upon its mouth as being wide open, one should cause the oblation (*āhuti*) to be offered there.
One should offer the oblation to the target so that it becomes manifest before one's eyes.
First, one should invoke Agni, who is worshipped by all the deities, who is adorned with divine garlands, who is fierce, and who accomplishes the awakening of the Buddhas. (4.26)
Oṃ, come,
come! You who must necessarily grant success directly within the fire—
fierce one, worshipped by the three worlds, saluted by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Having taken this water for the guest-offering (argha) and the water for the feet (pādya), together with the substances and the wielder of the vajra:
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
One should first offer the *argha* water and afterwards present the flower:
"Oṃ!
This divine flower is beautifully red, divinely fragrant, and most beautiful."
The lamp—illuminating, blazing, radiant, the remover of fear from the miserable realms, bestowing divine vision, and auspicious—he accepts this lamp. The mantra of the lamp. 4.30
Oṃ,
may he accept this auspicious sandalwood with camphor, along with lamps and fragrant incense that brings about his presence; remain present here.
The incense mantra: 4.31 Oṃ!
Various divine fragrances, adorned with various camphors.
"May this fragrance, produced from the various *hūṃ* syllables, be accepted.
First, the procedure for worship is firmly established by means of the fire;
afterwards, one should recite the *vidyā*, the mantra to be chanted, and one's own deity.
One should satisfy the Gaṇa, the Vidyā, and the practitioner themselves with offerings of song and dance in manifold ways,
if they desire accomplishment for themselves through the practice of body, speech, and mind. (4.34)
Having worshipped him, one should dismiss the deity—the fire, the wielder of the vajra, the Guru:
"Oṃ!
To Agni, the rite has been accomplished, which brings happiness to all sentient beings."

For the sake of accomplishing the perfection of body, speech, and mind, one must protect the deities. "Go, O Agni, with great gentleness; bring peace, O Mountain-dweller! [Bring peace] to all practitioners, both the stationary and the moving."
May the fruit of my merit become the bestower of mantra-siddhi. A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ E AI O AU AṂ AḤ HŪṂ HAḤ SVĀHĀ.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amṛta.

[He is] the Vajra-holder of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amṛta. This concludes the fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Ritual of Homa," in the *Vajrāmṛtamahātantra*.
[Chapter 5: Exposition on the Extent of Karma] The ritual procedure for the fire offering has been explained; now I shall describe to you the collyrium.
Take soot from a skull using a wick made of *mahāmeda*. 5.1
Having burned the head of an owl, one should saturate it with great blood;
then, having ground it well at night, one should have it made into fine powders. [Fol.
7 missing] Having completely filled [the vessel] with vulture’s feet...
[Chapter 6: Instruction on the Sadhana of Vajrahūṃkāra] One should depict him with four arms, two of which grasp the breasts;
all the vidyās have three faces, as do the gatekeepers and the goads. 6.6
One should likewise depict flowers, incense, lamps, and perfumes;
as well as Lāsyā, garlands, song, and dance for the six-armed one. On the flute, one should likewise depict all the vīṇās of Makunda and the others.
Likewise, all [the instruments] including the muraja drum should be depicted in the mandala.
In the *Vajrāmṛtamahātantra*, one should install the deities of the Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpika*);
indeed, each deity of the Fortunate Aeon has two arms and one face.
One should draw the practitioner in front, adorned with all ornaments;
likewise, one should draw a rosary, a vajra, and also a bell. [This is done] with offerings of bali and upahāra, and with the festivities of the taste of wine and drink.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should cast powder upon the mandala. Why not [cast] colored powders (*rajas*)?
Having prepared the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) in the center, one may attain whatever supreme accomplishment one desires.
One should accomplish the mantra of the all-pervasive Vajrahūṃkāra, which consists of a single syllable.
Afterwards, one should worship the preceptor, as well as oneself, the kingdom,
and even one's mother, sister, wife, and daughter.
If the mantra practitioner desires accomplishment for himself through the means of body, speech, and mind,
he should always practice that which is to be accomplished, which is the constant gateway to the three worlds.
The mandala of Vajrasattva, emerged from Vajrāmṛta, joined with the five nectars, is the destroyer of all miserable rebirths. || 6.15 ||
Through the union of the vajra-snap, the sādhanā of Śrī Vajrahūṃkāra has been taught; it is the miraculous manifestation of the bodhicitta within the yoga of the yoginīs. 6.16
One should perform the play of the Vidyā in the maṇḍala in many ways; having tasted [the essence] within the bhaga, the heroines are established in the mantra. 6.17.
One should kiss the lotus with the vajra, and likewise the nectar, which is the semen;
one must not extract it from that place, nor even with the fingers of both hands. (6.18)
Having extracted and destroyed [the seed-syllable], there is neither vigor nor indeed fruit;
having extracted the Great Vidyā and kissed the Vajrin.
His Buddhahood is accomplished as the immortal [essence] in the form of semen.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Vajrāmṛta of great bliss.
The Vajra-holder of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amṛta.
In the *Vajrāmṛtamahātantra*, this is the sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Sādhana of Vajra-Hūṃkāra."
Then the goddess Māmakī, established in amorous play, offered salutations with palms joined and recited this song: 7.1.
I bow to Vajrāmṛta, the hero with the body of Asitākṣa, surrounded by those who consider themselves heroes, and endowed with a multitude of mudrās. 7.2
I bow to Vajrāmṛta, who is attended by flocks of peacocks, resounded with the cries of cuckoos and bees, auspicious, and mounted upon sexual union. 7.3.
I bow to Vajrāmṛta, who is all, who is everything, who is formless, who is omniscient, and who is the friend of all, through the path of the perfectly disciplined senses. 7.4
The entire triple world, consisting of mind and the nectar of vajra, is without peer;
one should cause the twenty-four great vidyās to be impassioned with supreme passion.
I bow down to the glorious Vajrāmṛta, who has uprooted all afflictions, who is the abode established by all Buddhas, and who brings about all accomplishments. 7.6
O Nupparasa, you are a mantra; O Vajra, you are the goal of asceticism.
You are ever enamored with the auspiciousness of sexual union; you accomplish every task without exception.
O Supreme Lord, You are empty and stainless; You are the imperishable, the indestructible, and the unborn.
Afterwards, when this world of existence ceases to exist for You, how can there be any cycle of rebirth?
By means of this singing, through the transformations of the vajra-dance,
there are indeed the Bhāratī, Sāṃdhavī, and Nṛttasātvatī modes.
(Three verses from chapter 7 are quoted in the *Guṇavatī*) ...
CHAPTER 8. ŚRĪHERUKOTPATTINIRDEŚA (The Teaching on the Origin of Śrī Heruka)
[It is] surrounded. || 8.4 ||
He dwells in the great cremation ground, resounding with the sounds of mantras and *pheṭkāra* cries,
sporting with hosts of *bhūtas*, *vetālas*, and those who frequent the charnel grounds.
Then, the wielder of the great vajra should assume the form of Śrī Heruka while devouring the gods, including Indra, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. 8.6.
While being consumed, the first vidyā is Sotkaṭā, Vikaṭā, Cāṇḍālī, and Ḍombikā; Piṅgalā, Kulinī, Ugrā, and Dāruṇī is recorded as the eighth. || 8.7 ||
While this mantra is being recited, she, dancing, should cause it to be sung—
[the mantra] which is fierce with its stream of fangs, most terrifying, and adorned with a garland of entrails.
I bow down to Śrī Heruka, who is consuming great flesh;
I shall now proclaim the mantra to be recited for the benefit of practitioners. (8.9)
One should apply the third [note] to the third [syllable], the seventh to the fourth, and the seventh to the third; thus one should employ twelve syllables.
Joined with all the principles (tattvas) and adorned with the syllable *phaṭ*,
having extracted [the seed-syllable] from the sixth [vowel] and the fourth [consonant], the seat is formed by the first of the seventh [group].
One should extract the mantra ending in *svāhā*, pervaded by the thirteenth [vowel].
One should place Vairocana at the beginning; this is the root mantra for Heruka. (8.12)
And hear, O Māmakī, the majesty of this king of mantras:
by reciting the mantra even once, one may destroy the three worlds in an instant.
One should consume the three realms without remainder, free from hesitation;
for she indeed grants all desires, and one shall become equal to Śrī Heruka. 8.14
"It is not *aluk*, but rather the augment *num* or *ṇum," so said the Blessed Lord Vajrī, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amṛta;

the Vajrī of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amṛta. This is the eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Arising of Śrī Heruka," in the *Vajrāmṛtamahātantra*. O ||
CHAPTER 9. AMṚTAKUṆḌALIN Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalin.
(Understand: *kuṇḍaleḥ*)
Three-faced and six-armed, fierce, with a complexion like black crushed collyrium.
He was surrounded by garlands of flames, fierce, with tawny eyes and glowing tawny hair,
overcome by great obstacles, and holding a raised axe in his hand.
With his left hand, he holds a raised axe, a pestle, a thunderbolt, and a noose,
while pointing with his index finger.
Threatening all the wicked with his index finger, one should visualize a sword in [the deity's] hand. 9.3.
One should meditate upon the secret lotus as being joined with the eight vidyās and Lakṣmī, accompanied by the gatekeepers; one should then place the eight vidyās upon the petals.
Amṛtā, Amṛtavajrā, Amṛtā, and Amṛtalocanā; Aprameyā, Surūpā, Vāruṇā, and Sukhasādhanī. || 9.5 ||
All [the deities] in the cardinal and intermediate directions have three faces and six arms;
with lotuses raised in their hands, they dance together with the Goddess, bestowing the manifestation of universal forms.
While laughing and exclaiming "kilikila," one should recollect the King of Mantras;
then one should bestow Vairocana and fulfill that state. 9.7
The first [syllable] is the second [vowel], joined with the void and the seat;
the void is stepped upon by the void, and the mantra is joined at the end with *svāhā*.
Through the unions of supreme passion, the nectar arises as nectar;
by means of the yoga of nectar, one should accomplish the Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever remembers Amṛtakuṇḍalin will, by means of all the siddhis, accomplish all goals without delay. 9.10
At the time of his dance, O Vajrāmṛta, he meditates upon the entire triple world, with all its moving and unmoving beings, within the palm of his hand, in great bliss.

The Vajra-holder of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amṛta. This is the ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Arising of Śrī Amṛtakuṇḍalī," in the *Vajrāmṛtamahātantra*. Oṃ.
Chapter 10: The Accomplishment of the Vetāla.
Now I shall explain another [practice], the great accomplishment of the Vetāla.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at a solitary linga or at a crossroads, [one should proceed].
One should accomplish all rites as well as the rite for raising up a *vetāla* at a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, on a riverbank, or on a mountain; likewise,
[one should take] a woman who died by hanging and who is endowed with all auspicious marks.
Mātaṅgī, Ḍombīkā, Śvapākī, Nirvraṇā, and Cāruśobhanā; Nirvraṇā is the thirtieth, while Saumyā has given birth to twenty-five. Among children, the dead woman is seized.
One should bathe [the deity] with divine water mixed with mantras and medicinal herbs;
one should perform anointing upon it with white sandalwood and camphor;
one should worship with flowers and incense and cause various offerings to be presented.
Having anointed [the ground] with great oil, the practitioner of Śrī Heruka should strike the face [of the site] with mustard seeds; there he should draw a mandala,
filling it with a half-moon known as a skull and shaped like a bow.
Endowed with the eight sciences and adorned with skull-cups,
they all hold khaṭvāṅgas;
possessing three faces, they are of fierce appearance, with six arms and swords in their hands.
Outside this mandala, one should appoint the gatekeepers:
Gokarṇa, Hastikarṇa, Sumukha, and likewise Durmukha.
They hold nooses and goads, are fierce, hideous, formidable, and terrifying.
One should depict [the goddess] with two arms and one face for the worship with flowers;
that Vidyā, however, should depict the various worship of the maṇḍala.
Then the heroic practitioner should assume a form resembling Heruka.
Having adorned herself with great conchs and a crest of a garland of skulls,
she should carry a hand-drum while dancing as she enters the city;
she should bear it with mantras and cause it to be sounded there with the syllable *phaṭ*.

One should worship the divine mandala and sprinkle it with great red [sindūra]. While reciting the great mantra of Śrī Heruka, the practitioner should utter the roar of the Vetāḍa, resounding like one possessed by wrath.
He should not be afraid then; the practitioner should recollect Śrī Heruka.
Having arisen, the Vetāla said this to the practitioner:
"O Great Hero, what is your task? Give me the command of the Vajrin!"
For a practitioner who desires to conquer the sword, collyrium, the underworld, or the power of moving through the sky,
he should accomplish that very rite for the sake of the seeker. Then the practitioner should perform whatever is desired by the mind of whichever [seeker].
Māmakī, as the root-lotus, shall accomplish all things;
she brings about the primary siddhi of the vetāla issued from the Vajrāmṛta,
which bestows happiness upon practitioners for the sake of accomplishing the goals of body, speech, and mind.

Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the great bliss of vajra-amṛta; the great bliss of the vajra-body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. This is the tenth chapter, the exposition titled "The Accomplishment of the Vetāla," in the *Vajrāmṛtamahātantra*. O ||
Chapter 11: "The Five Nectars" (Pañcāmṛta) Then the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the great bliss of vajra-nectar, remained silent, established in the union of the vajra and the lotus. 11.1
When Aśvasena and Kampa gazed upon him but did not speak,
having entered the supreme meditative absorption, Māmakī asked again:
"The Blessed One, the subtle vajra, abides in the hearts of all sentient beings."

"How, by what manner, is that reality perceived? Then the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amita, opening his eyes, spoke these words while laughing: 11.3–4. "How, by what manner, is that reality perceived? Then the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Amita, opening his eyes, spoke these words while laughing.
Previously, however, the reality was described as the nectar in the form of semen;
one should always and constantly taste it together with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
O Māmakī, hear now the greatness of each of these substances individually.
First, one should consume the semen, which is the means for accomplishing knowledge and the object of knowledge.
For the sake of attaining perfection of body, speech, and mind, one should prepare the "great blood.
One should always take that from a maiden, or even from whoever is dear to oneself.
For this [deity] accomplishes all tasks; Māmakī, however, is intensely red.
Having obtained one born of death, one should take his great flesh—whether it be someone impaled on a stake or even one slain in battle. (11.8)
One should consume that which is firm and profound, which increases longevity and health,
grants desires and happiness, and accomplishes the awakening of a Buddha;
it is as inexhaustible as Vajrasattva and bestows the fruits of all desires.

One should consume adamantine water and excrement, as well as the knowledge of the self; having then made them into a fine powder, one should saturate it with great blood. This should always be performed at dawn, as well as at dusk and at midday.

The yogi should consume [it] three times a day and then drink vajra-water. Furthermore, the practitioner who accomplishes Māmakī day after day will have a body free from disease, which destroys old age and illness. || 11.12–11.13 ||
Good fortune, a beautiful form, splendor, and victory at the royal gate;
for them, the exhaustion of all desires is attained, as well as the most excellent reality.
He is a yogi, he is omniscient, endowed with the qualities of Vajrasattva.
Freed from passion and hatred, and devoid of greed and envy,
his practice succeeds— the great bliss of Vajrāmṛta.
This *Vajrāmṛta-tantra* is vast in extent and its profound meaning is hidden.
[folio 12 recto] Herein, the entirety of the Vajrayāna has emerged from the Goddess.
(11.16) This reality, the true being, impassioned by supreme passion, has not been told by me to anyone; it is Māmakī, the gross lotus. (11.17)

This supreme secret, delightful and ever-abiding within the self of all, is formless, empty, and imperishable; it was not realized by the Bodhisattva. This is the reality of the Great Vidyā, known as the Vajra-Cūḍāmaṇi.
One should hold [this] secret, O Goddess; one should not place trust even in father or son.
This reality should be given to a hero who is extremely guarded, devoted to the Guru, and firm in his vows, if he desires supreme enlightenment.
This *Vajrāmṛta* tantra is easy to accomplish yet very difficult to find;
one should practice it, O fortunate one, as a gentle compendium of the essence of knowledge.
That practitioner who has been consecrated in this great *Vajrāmṛta* tantra—
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and everyone else, pay homage to him.
Having paid homage three times a day to the Teacher, the most fortunate one, [he says]:
"You alone are the Lord who delivers all sentient beings from saṃsāra. (11.22–23)
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Immortality;
the Vajra-holder of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, the Great Bliss of Vajra-Immortality.
O Dear One, the deposition of the Great Tantra of Vajra-Immortality has been told.
Then the Vajra-holder abides in the form of the *bhaga* as a subtle form.

Thus ends the eleventh explanatory tantra, titled "The Means for Accomplishing the Five Nectars," from the *Vajrāmṛtamahātantra*. [Floral Ornament] The Great Reality of Vajrāmṛta, which accomplishes the awakening of the Buddhas. Om.
In the year 282, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, on a Saturday.
